clinicalPearls: C6 is a terminal complement component; its absence prevents assembly of a functional membrane attack complex, so the hallmark presentation is recurrent or unusually severe neisserial disease.
Recurrent meningococcal meningitis or meningococcaemia, often caused by uncommon serogroups (such as W, X, Y or 29E) rather than the typical epidemic serogroups, should prompt suspicion.
Infections tend to begin in later childhood or adolescence and may recur across a lifetime, in contrast to the very early-onset infections of some early-component defects.
The screening test of choice is the total haemolytic complement assay (CH50/CH100), which is undetectable or profoundly low because the classical pathway cannot complete lysis.
AH50 (alternative pathway haemolytic assay) is also abnormal, helping localise the block to a shared terminal component rather than an early classical-pathway protein.
Meningococcal disease in these patients is often less fulminant with lower case-fatality than in the general population, but recurrences are characteristic and can still cause significant morbidity.
Immunisation against Neisseria meningitidis (including conjugate and serogroup B vaccines) and against other encapsulated organisms is the cornerstone of prevention.
Inheritance is autosomal recessive; screening and counselling of siblings and other first-degree relatives is warranted after a proband is identified.
reference.pathophysiology: Complement Component 6 deficiency arises from biallelic loss-of-function variants in the C6 gene, encoding a terminal complement protein. C6 combines with C5b to initiate assembly of the membrane attack complex (MAC, C5b-9); together with C7, C8 and multiple C9 molecules it forms the lytic transmembrane pore that directly kills Gram-negative organisms, most importantly Neisseria species. Without functional C6, the C5b-7 intermediate cannot form and the terminal lytic pathway is interrupted, so complement-mediated bacteriolysis fails even though opsonisation (C3b) and anaphylatoxin generation (C3a, C5a) via the upstream cascade remain intact. Because Neisseria are especially dependent on direct serum bactericidal killing by the MAC, the clinical phenotype is dominated by susceptibility to meningococcal and, less often, disseminated gonococcal infection. A relatively common subtotal (dysfunctional) allele and combined C6/C7 deficiency due to adjacent gene defects are also described. The defect is quantitative or qualitative for a single terminal protein, so the remainder of innate and adaptive immunity is preserved.
additionalDifferentials: C8 deficiency (alpha-gamma or beta chain) with similar neisserial susceptibility
C5 deficiency affecting both MAC formation and C5a-mediated chemotaxis
C9 deficiency, which is often milder as partial lysis can still occur
Properdin deficiency causing X-linked fulminant meningococcal disease
Asplenia or hyposplenism predisposing to encapsulated organism sepsis
Primary antibody deficiency presenting with recurrent encapsulated bacterial infection
additionalInvestigations: Total classical-pathway haemolytic assay (CH50/CH100) as the initial screen
Alternative-pathway haemolytic assay (AH50) to localise a terminal-component block
Specific C6 antigenic and functional level to confirm the deficient component
Sequencing of the C6 gene to identify the causative variant and confirm zygosity
Culture and serogrouping of Neisseria meningitidis from blood or cerebrospinal fluid
Measurement of remaining terminal components (C5, C7, C8, C9) to exclude combined deficiency
Family screening of siblings with a haemolytic complement assay
redFlags: Recurrent episodes of meningococcal meningitis or meningococcaemia
Invasive neisserial infection caused by uncommon serogroups
A first-degree relative with recurrent or fatal meningococcal disease
New febrile illness with headache, neck stiffness or a non-blanching rash in a known deficient patient
Undetectable CH50/CH100 on repeat testing outside an acute consumptive illness
reference.prognosis: With prompt recognition of infection, appropriate vaccination and rapid antimicrobial treatment of acute episodes, long-term outlook is good and meningococcal disease in affected individuals often carries a lower case-fatality than in the general population. Recurrent infection remains the principal lifelong risk, so sustained preventive measures and patient education are essential.
pitfalls: Attributing a single episode of meningococcal disease to bad luck and failing to screen complement after invasive neisserial infection, especially with rare serogroups.
Testing CH50 on an improperly handled or old sample, giving a falsely low result and mislabelling a healthy person as deficient.
Assuming vaccination alone abolishes risk; breakthrough infection can still occur and warrants a high index of suspicion for any febrile illness.
Overlooking combined C6/C7 deficiency because only one component was measured.
Failing to counsel and screen at-risk relatives once a proband is diagnosed.
references: Standard clinical immunology textbook, current edition
National immunisation guidance for asplenic and complement-deficient patients
Peer-reviewed reviews of terminal complement deficiency and neisserial disease
management: Vaccinate against meningococcus with quadrivalent conjugate (ACWY) and serogroup B vaccines and keep boosters current, recognising that infections often involve uncommon serogroups.
Keep pneumococcal and Haemophilus influenzae type b immunisations up to date.
Treat febrile illness promptly with empirical antibiotics covering Neisseria meningitidis, confirming the serogroup by culture and PCR.
Consider prophylactic penicillin for recurrent neisserial disease.
Educate patient and family in early recognition of meningococcal disease and provide rapid-access care.
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive defect and screen relatives, noting the possibility of combined C6/C7 deficiency.
